Mount Tambora. An active stratovolcano on the island of Sumbawa in Indonesia, Mount Tambora is the site of the largest volcanic eruption in recorded human history. It erupted in April 1815, which remains the largest and most destructive volcanic eruption in recorded history, ejecting an estimated 160 cubic kilometers of material. The explosion had a Volcanic Explosivity Index of seven and injected vast amounts of volcanic ash and sulfur into the stratosphere, killing over 70,000 people directly and through subsequent famine. The eruption caused the Year Without a Summer in 1816, as stratospheric aerosol clouds blocked sunlight, causing widespread crop failures, food riots, and unseasonable summer snowstorms in New England and Western Europe. The eruption inspired the writing of Frankenstein, which Mary Shelley drafted during the cold, wet, and gloomy summer of 1816 while vacationing with Lord Byron at Lake Geneva. Mount Tambora completely decimated the indigenous Tambora culture, wiping out a small agricultural kingdom on Sumbawa and causing the extinction of its unique, non-Austronesian language. The eruption left a massive summit caldera measuring over four miles wide and 3,600 feet deep, which reduced the mountain's height from approximately 14,000 feet to 9,350 feet. Mount Tambora connects to Krakatoa, another Indonesian stratovolcano whose 1883 eruption was also famous for its explosive force and global effects, and to Mount Pinatubo, a modern Philippine volcano that caused a similar, though less severe, global temperature drop in 1991.
